11.0.s.en: (1) David's successive victories over the children of Ammon

11.0.0.en: After the year was expired: after a year had passed.

11.0.1.en: At the time when kings go forth to battle: at the time of the year when kings usually go out to wage wars, which is spring or summer, when the weather is suitable.

11.0.2.en: Rabbah: the capital of the children of Ammon, situated on the Jabbok River, a tributary of the Jordan.

11.0.3.en: When David saw that the children of Ammon were not submitting to him like the rest of the surrounding lands, and that they were trying to renew their strength and prepare for war, he decided, a year after fighting them and the Arameans, to wage a third war on the children of Ammon, to discipline them and break them completely, so that they would no longer think of stirring up war against the children of Israel again. He put Joab at the head of the army, together with the men of war from all the tribes of Israel, and they destroyed their cities and lands and besieged their capital “Rabbah.” This time David did not go out to war with his army but remained in Jerusalem.

11.0.4.en: Thus David triumphed over the enemies surrounding the kingdom of the children of Israel and subdued them in seven wars, which are:

11.0.6.en: 2- The war against the Philistines and their allies alone.

11.0.10.en: 6- The war against the children of Ammon and Aram.

11.0.11.en: May you put an end to everything connected with sin, and keep nothing that reminds you of it, lest Satan use it against you in your time of weakness; and give up anything that binds you to sin, however dear it may be to you.

11.1.0.en: This chapter and the next speak of the great sin into which David fell, which left an evil mark upon him and upon his house. After David had eaten his midday meal and rested a little, he rose to walk a while on the roof of his house, and he saw a woman of surpassing beauty bathing in a place near his house; and when his eyes fell upon her, he desired her in his heart.

11.1.1.en: David abandoned his striving with his army and gave himself over to idleness, and so he fell into sin. Perhaps this gives us a strong lesson to continue always in our striving, to avoid what is unbecoming to the children of God, and to shun the idleness that may be an open door to practices that do not please the Lord.

11.2.0.en: Bathsheba the daughter of Eliam: she is also called “Bath-shua the daughter of Ammiel,” as is recorded in (1 Chr 3:5); her first son died and the second was Solomon.

11.2.1.en: David asked those around him who this woman was, and he was told that she was Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite. He was one of the heroes of David's army (ch. 23:39), and was originally a pagan of the sons of Heth but became a Jew, or his father became a Jew and so he became a Jew.

11.3.0.en: David sent and summoned Bathsheba to his house, and perhaps he showed his servants that he wished to inquire after her welfare because she was the wife of one of the chief commanders of his army. He was alone with her and caressed her until he slipped and lay with her. She had finished the seven days of her menstruation (her monthly period), during which she was unclean according to the Law and no one could touch her (Lev 12:1), and he supposed, according to expectation, that conception could not occur immediately after the seven days.

11.3.1.en: We must take care for true purity and not merely outward purity, and not do as David did, who was careful not to touch Bathsheba during the days of her menstruation but did what was far worse, because his heart had already been defiled within; so he caressed her until he committed adultery with her. Therefore let us train ourselves to control our senses, because through them sin enters, which defiles body and spirit together.

11.4.0.en: The fruit of sin soon appeared, and the woman conceived. This was a great predicament, exposing her to death by the judgment of the Law (Lev 20:10), so she sent to David to tell him of the situation that he might rescue her. Thus we see the justice of God, who permitted David to be exposed although the likelihood of conception was very slight, so that David and all generations might know the importance of vigilance and of keeping away from sin, even if it could be hidden from the eyes of people.

11.5.s.en: (3) The failure of the attempt to cover the sin

11.5.0.en: David thought, and his thinking led him to a plan which he supposed would bring him out of this predicament. He sent to the commander of his army, Joab, to send Uriah to him, and Joab did so and sent Uriah to him.

11.6.0.en: Uriah carried out the order summoning him to the king, not knowing the reason for it. David told him that, because of his trust in him and his knowledge of his ability to judge rightly the military situation of the battle raging against the children of Ammon, he had summoned him in order to ask him about the progress of the war, the welfare of Joab, and the welfare of the army.

11.7.0.en: Wash thy feet: to wash after the long journey.

11.7.1.en: A mess of meat: a portion of food.

11.7.2.en: David showed great hospitality to Uriah, permitting him to go to his house and wash after the toils of the long journey, and as soon as he left him, he sent after him a choice portion of delicious food so that he and his wife might eat. But in reality this honor was not for Uriah; David's aim was that he should spend the night with his wife, so that people would think that Bathsheba's child was Uriah's, and thereby he would hide his sin.

11.8.0.en: Uriah did not wish to go to his house to sleep there, but spent his night in one of the rooms set apart for the lodging of the royal guard, which were beside the gate of the royal palace.

11.9.0.en: Some of David's men told him that Uriah had not gone to his house to sleep there, and David was bewildered by the matter and asked him why he had not taken advantage of being near his house to rest in it with his wife. David's agitation appears here because of his fear that his sin would be exposed, and perhaps this agitation was evident to those around him; for these are the inevitable results of sin.

11.10.0.en: Uriah answered him that it was not fitting for him to lodge in his house with his wife while the ark of the covenant of the Lord was in a tent, and the soldiers of the children of Israel, whether of the tribe of Judah or of the other tribes, and Joab the commander of the army, were all lodging in tents they had pitched in the open field near the battlefield; so how, this being the case, could he allow himself to rest and take his ease with his wife? And he swore by the life of the king that he would not do this.

11.11.0.en: David gave him leave for another day, on condition that he would let him return to the battlefield after the two days had passed, so Uriah stayed in Jerusalem another day in compliance with the king's order. We wonder here why David gave him leave for another day when Uriah was occupied with thoughts of the war, because he was an important commander among David's commanders. Of course the reason is clear: perhaps he would long to see his wife and go into his house, and there would be an opportunity for him to lie with her, and so David would hide his sin.

11.12.0.en: After David had given Uriah the opportunity of another day, he noticed that he had not gone into his house, so he invited him to eat the midday meal with him, and deliberately made him drink much wine until he was drunk, and he went out from David's presence at evening. David thought that, with Uriah having lost his senses, he would long for his wife and go to his house in a state of drunkenness and lie with her; but Uriah's subconscious mind was occupied with the war and with fulfilling his duty as a commander for God's sake, so that even when he was drunk he did not return to his house but slept with the king's servants.

11.12.1.en: Sin is sinful and its results are distressing, so do not be drawn to its desire, for within its honey is poison. Keep away from every source of sin, however small it may seem, and you will live in purity and enjoy peace, and you will be able to be with God and to carry out your work successfully.

11.13.s.en: (4) The killing of Uriah in the war

11.13.0.en: When David's attempts with Uriah failed, he thought of another scheme. He sent a written letter, sealed and closed, to Joab by the hand of Uriah, telling him in it to set Uriah in the forefront of the ranks when the battle grew fierce, and to order the rest of his soldiers to withdraw from around him so that he would receive the blows alone, be struck, and die. Here we see how cruel David was and how unjust to an innocent man who carried in his own hand the letter of his death like one carrying his own shroud, and this shows how sin drags other sins along with it.

11.13.1.en: Let us beware of the first step and be aware of how sin enters a person gradually, for as soon as one falls into a single sin, it drags after it many sins. David's sin began with a look, and then the other sins followed in its train, so that there was the sin of adultery, then murder.

11.14.0.en: Joab obeyed the king's order. When he besieged the city of “Rabbah of Ammon,” the capital of the Ammonites, he put Uriah at the head of the army in the most difficult position, opposite the strongest men of the enemy, and then ordered his men to withdraw from around Uriah and leave him alone to face the enemy forces.

11.14.1.en: The enemy's soldiers came out to defend their capital, and some of the soldiers of the army of Israel were killed, among them Uriah the Hittite.

11.14.2.en: And here we see how Joab carried out David's words with skill, not only in obedience to the king, but in order to catch him in a fault, namely murder, so that David would no longer rebuke him for killing Abner; and thus Joab shared with David in the sin of murder. For whoever falls into sin wants to justify himself by seeing those around him fallen into sin, so that his conscience may not reproach him and he may not repent.

11.14.3.en: David felt humiliated and weak before Joab and could not harm him despite his evil deeds, so he charged his son Solomon to repay him according to his deeds (1 Kgs 2:5, 6). And we note Joab's strength in rebuking David after Joab killed Absalom, when David did not speak to him for fear of him (ch. 19:5-8).

11.15.0.en: Joab sent a message to the king informing him that his orders concerning the military plans had been fully carried out, and telling him the state of the battles in progress and the remaining details of the war against the children of Ammon.

11.16.0.en: His message was oral, and he charged the messenger to observe the effect of his words on the king: if he found that the king was displeased because they had come near the wall of the city of Rabbah, he was to tell him that Uriah was among those killed. This was because Joab knew in his shrewdness that the king would understand that it was a deliberate plan to be rid of Uriah according to the king's own orders. They should not have approached the walls, because the enemy hurled huge stones to strike the soldiers besieging the city, and it would have been better to besiege it from a distance. The king might remind the messenger of the death of Abimelech the son of Gideon, who was besieging his enemies in the tower of the city of “Thebez,” when a woman cast a piece of a millstone upon him from the top of the wall and broke his skull (Judg 9:

11.16.1.en: 50-54.) (Joab ordered his messenger that, if he noticed David's anger at what he reported to him.

11.17.0.en: The messenger left the field of battle and went to Jerusalem, making for the king's house, and told the king all that Joab had sent him with.

11.18.0.en: The messenger related the details of the events to the king, saying that the enemy had prevailed against them when they went out from the city into the plain to fight them there, and the soldiers of Israel launched a counterattack that forced the enemy to fall back to the entrance of the city, which brought the soldiers of Israel close to the wall of the city, and the enemy took advantage of this position to shoot arrows at them from the wall. Perhaps the messenger noticed the king's displeasure at the situation, and so he hastened to tell him of the death of Uriah.

11.19.0.en: David was relieved when he heard of Uriah's death, and the signs of anger vanished from his face. He charged the messenger with a reply to Joab, telling him not to be grieved over the killing of a number of his soldiers, for on the battlefields everyone is exposed to death. He added in his message that Joab must take courage and fight against the city strongly until the army of Israel entered it and destroyed it. Then he charged the messenger to encourage Joab and strengthen his resolve on behalf of the king.

11.20.0.en: The inhabitants of Jerusalem learned, from following the news of their army, that Uriah had died. Bathsheba his wife learned the news of his death, and she did what custom required of her of lamenting and weeping, regardless of her inner feeling.

11.21.0.en: The mourning: a period of usually seven days, like the mourning for Saul (1 Sam 31:13). After the mourning for Uriah ended and the days of grief were complete, David married Bathsheba and she bore him a son. The Lord was greatly displeased at David's falling into the sin of defilement, for it was not fitting to answer God's work on his behalf by breaking His commandments, especially since adultery had drawn him into cruelty, to the point that he killed a great and innocent commander among the commanders of his war to cover his shameful sin.

11.21.1.en: Believers must keep their purity, for they are temples of God and the Spirit of God dwells in them, so let them not anger God by an ugly deed. Is it fitting that we answer God's saving work on our behalf by breaking His commandments? God was displeased at what David did of adultery and murder for the following reasons:

11.21.2.en: 1- Because God raised him from behind the sheep and made him a great king, why then should he betray God by breaking His commandments?!

11.21.3.en: 2- David was greatly godly in his righteousness, so why did this great tower fall and accept a great sin like adultery?

11.21.4.en: 3- God favored David with the presence of the ark in his city so that he might remember God's constant presence with him, but he neglected this and fell into his grievous sin.

11.21.5.en: 4- David was an example and a model for his people because he was the king; by his falling into sin he became very small in the eyes of Joab the head of his army and in the eyes of many of his servants, who drew conclusions and understood the matter, and he made them stumble greatly.

11.21.6.en: 5- David's age at that time was about fifty, which is the age of settledness, that is, without the impulsiveness of youth, so it is strange that he fell into this sin.

11.21.7.en: 6- David was married to several women, so there was no need for him to look at another woman.

11.21.8.en: And by David's falling into adultery, he fell into a group of sins, which are:

11.21.9.en: 1- He forgot that he was the Lord's anointed, consecrated to His service by leading his kingdom, so it was not right for him to submit to evil desires.

11.21.10.en: 2- He neglected the sense of the importance of fighting for God's sake; for if he had grown old and could not go out, he should at least have prayed for the fighters and not sought in his selfishness his own pleasure.

11.21.11.en: 3- He wronged this woman and drew her into sin, for she may have been affected by his position and feared to oppose him.

11.21.12.en: 4- He betrayed one of his military commanders by assaulting his wife, especially since he was a foreigner who had become a Jew, and so was exposed to severe stumbling.

11.21.13.en: 5- The sin of adultery drew him to the sin of murder in order to hide his crime, so he killed an innocent man.

11.21.14.en: 6- Most important, he broke the Law of God and became condemned to death.

11.21.15.en: 7- Laxity toward the evil look and the wicked thought, which led him to complete fall into adultery.

11.21.16.en: 8- Idleness and slackness: after he had eaten he rose to walk on his roof, and so he became exposed to falling into sin.

11.21.17.en: The humility of the Christ is shown in His being pleased to be born of the descendants of Bathsheba, who committed adultery with David (Mt 1:

11.21.18.en: 6), to declare that He came to save adulterers and sinners by His redemption of them on the Cross.

11.21.19.en: David's punishment, and then his capture of Rabbah of the children of Ammon
